Security professionals everywhere use one simple model to describe what they are protecting: the **CIA triad**. It has nothing to do with spies. The letters stand for **Confidentiality**, **Integrity** and **Availability**. Every security problem you will ever handle damages at least one of these three, and naming which one helps you choose the right fix.

Four attack patterns you will meet most often
Advanced attacks exist, but small businesses, schools, churches and NGOs are mostly hurt by four ordinary patterns. Learn these well and you can protect most of what matters.
list
**Account takeover:** an attacker gets into an email, social media or banking account, usually with a password that was reused from another site that leaked, or one typed into a fake login page.
**Business email compromise (BEC):** the attacker uses a real or lookalike email account to ask for a payment, a change of bank details or sensitive documents. Lesson 2 covers it in depth.
**Ransomware and other malware:** harmful software, often arriving through a pirated program, a fake update or an email attachment, that steals data or encrypts files and demands payment.
**Lost, stolen or shared devices and accounts:** a phone with no screen lock, a shared office password that former staff still know, or a flash drive with client files left in a cybercafé.

The common thread is that none of these needs a genius attacker. Each one exploits a habit or a missing control: a reused password, no second factor, no backup, no offboarding. That is good news, because habits and controls are things you can change in an afternoon.
How an account takeover actually unfolds
diagram
Account takeover, stage by stage
Password leaks or is phished
Attacker logs in quietly
Sets forwarding or recovery changes
Reads mail, studies contacts
Sends fraud or locks owner out
Each stage is a chance to stop the attack: unique passwords stop stage one, a second factor stops stage two, and regular checks catch stage three.

The quiet middle stages are the part most people never hear about. A careful attacker does not shout. They add a rule that silently forwards copies of every email to an outside address, or change the recovery phone number so the real owner cannot reset the password later. Then they read for days or weeks, learning who pays whom, before acting. This is why a security lead checks forwarding rules and recovery settings, not only passwords.

Worked example: classifying three incidents

For example, Amaka has just been asked to be the volunteer IT lead for a women's cooperative in Owerri with 9 staff. In her first week the coordinator tells her about three things that happened last year.

Incident A: the cooperative's Facebook page was taken over and posted fake loan adverts for two days. Amaka classifies it as **integrity** (false content published in the cooperative's name) and **availability** (staff could not use the page). Pattern: account takeover.

Incident B: the treasurer received an email that looked like it came from the chairperson, asking for an urgent transfer of 350,000 naira to a "new vendor". Pattern: business email compromise, an attack on **integrity** of the instruction. It was stopped only because the treasurer phoned the chairperson.

Incident C: the old office laptop, holding scanned membership forms with National Identification Numbers, was given to a relative without being wiped. Pattern: device handling. Property: **confidentiality**.
She writes one line per incident: what happened, triad property, pattern, and the missing control (no second factor on Facebook, no payment call-back rule, no device wiping procedure).
Amaka now has three concrete gaps to fix, ranked by harm, instead of a vague feeling that "we need better security". This list becomes the first input to the risk register in Lesson 3.
callout
Security is about trade-offs

Perfect confidentiality (lock everything away) can destroy availability (nobody can do their work). Your job is not to remove all risk but to bring it down to a level the organisation accepts, at a cost it can afford.

**Social engineering** means manipulating people, rather than computers, into giving access, money or information. It works because it uses normal human instincts: respect for authority, wanting to help, fear of trouble and hurry. At the organisational level you must go past "don't click strange links" and understand how targeted attacks are built, so that you can design processes that stop them even when someone is fooled.

Business email compromise in five moves

Business email compromise, or BEC, is one of the most costly forms of fraud for organisations because it ends in a real bank transfer that is hard to reverse. It usually follows this sequence: the attacker gains access to, or imitates, an email account; studies who pays whom; waits for a real transaction; inserts a request to change bank details or pay urgently; and pressures the payer to act before checking.
Business email compromise sequence
Access or imitate a mailbox
Study who pays whom
Wait for a real invoice
Request bank-detail change
Pressure for fast payment
Breaking any link stops the fraud, and the cheapest link to break is the last one: a fixed rule to verify before paying.
Reading an email like an investigator

The name you see on an email is just a label the sender types. What matters is the actual address and what the receiving server found when it checked the message. In Gmail on a computer, open the message, click the three dots and choose **Show original**. You will see the full headers, including a summary line for SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
**From address:** look at the full address, not the display name. "Chairperson Ada" <ada.chair.office@gmail.com> is not the cooperative's real domain.
**Reply-To:** a different Reply-To address means your answer goes somewhere else. This is a common BEC trick.
**Lookalike domains:** swapped letters (rn for m), extra words (-ng, -office) or a different ending (.co instead of .org).
**SPF** (Sender Policy Framework): the domain publishes which servers are allowed to send its mail. A FAIL means the sending server was not on the list.
**DKIM** (DomainKeys Identified Mail): a digital signature proving the message was not altered and came through the domain's own system.
**DMARC**: the domain owner's instruction on what to do when SPF or DKIM checks fail (do nothing, send to spam, or reject), plus reports back to the owner.
Passing checks does not mean safe

If the attacker is inside a real, hacked mailbox, SPF, DKIM and DMARC will all PASS because the email truly came from that account. Authentication tells you where a message came from, not whether the person behind it is honest. That is why the payment rule below is your strongest defence.
Worked example: dissecting a bank-detail change request

For example, Funmi is finance officer for a small Abuja training NGO. On a Thursday afternoon she receives an email from "Musa, Brightline Printers" saying their bank has changed and the pending invoice of 2,450,000 naira (illustrative amount) should go to a new account today to avoid a late fee.

She checks the From address: musa@brightline-printers.com. The supplier's usual address, from past invoices, is musa@brightlineprinters.com.ng. The hyphen and the different ending are a lookalike domain.
She opens Show original. SPF and DKIM pass, but for brightline-printers.com, a domain the attacker owns. The checks prove only that the attacker sent it from their own domain.
The Reply-To is a third address on a free mail service.
The email quotes the correct invoice number, which means someone has seen the real invoice. She suspects the supplier's mailbox, or her own, has been compromised.
She does not reply. She calls Musa on the phone number saved from the original contract, not the number in the email. Musa confirms his bank details have not changed.
She reports the email to her IT lead, who checks her mailbox for forwarding rules and warns the supplier that their account may be hacked.
No money is lost. The NGO adds a written rule: any change to a payee's bank details must be confirmed by a call to a number already on file and approved by a second person before payment.
A payment verification rule that works
steps
Keep a supplier master list with bank details and phone numbers collected at onboarding.
Treat any request to change bank details, by any channel, as suspicious until verified.
Verify by calling a number already on file, never one supplied in the request.
Require a second approver for new payees and for any payment above a set threshold.
Wait a fixed cooling-off period (for example, one working day) for first payments to a changed account.
Record the verification: date, who called, who confirmed.
If a transfer has already gone out, speed matters. Call your bank's fraud line at once and ask them to contact the receiving bank, then follow the incident steps you will build in Module 2.

You cannot protect everything equally, so security leads use **risk assessment** to decide where effort goes first. A risk is a combination of three things: an **asset** you care about, a **threat** that could harm it, and a **vulnerability** (a weakness) that lets the threat succeed. Remove any one of the three and the risk falls.
Step one: the asset inventory

List what the organisation would be hurt to lose, leak or have altered. Think in four groups: information (member lists, payroll, donor records), accounts (email, bank, social media, domain name), devices (laptops, phones, routers), and services (website, cloud storage, accounting software). For each, record the owner, where it lives and who has access.
private-data
A person beside a large document protected by a lock
Personal data about members, staff and clients is usually the most sensitive asset a small organisation holds.
Step two: score each risk

For every important asset, name a realistic threat and score two things on a scale of 1 to 5. **Likelihood**: 1 is rare, 5 is almost certain within a year. **Impact**: 1 is minor inconvenience, 5 is severe harm to people, money or the organisation's survival. Multiply them to get a risk score from 1 to 25.
Likelihood and impact matrix
Low likelihood, high impact: plan for it
High likelihood, high impact: act now
Low likelihood, low impact: accept and watch
High likelihood, low impact: quick fixes
Likelihood (1 to 5)
Impact (1 to 5)
Scores in the top-right quadrant get controls first; the bottom-left can usually be accepted and reviewed later.

A common rule of thumb: scores of 15 to 25 are high and need action now, 8 to 14 are medium and need a plan with a date, and 1 to 7 are low and can be accepted and reviewed. Your organisation can set its own bands, but write them down so decisions are consistent.
Worked example: a five-line risk register
For example, Amaka (from Lesson 1) scores the women's cooperative's main risks on a sheet with columns: asset, threat, vulnerability, likelihood, impact, score, control, owner, due date.

Main email account, taken over through a reused password, no second factor: likelihood 4 × impact 5 = **20 (high)**. Control: unique password in a password manager plus authenticator app. Owner: coordinator. Due: this week.
Supplier payments, BEC bank-detail change, no call-back rule: 3 × 5 = **15 (high)**. Control: written verification rule. Owner: treasurer.
Member records on one laptop, ransomware or theft, no backup: 3 × 4 = **12 (medium)**. Control: encrypted cloud backup plus an offline copy. Due: within 30 days.
Facebook page, takeover, two admins share one login: 3 × 3 = **9 (medium)**. Control: separate personal admin accounts with two-step verification.
Office Wi-Fi, a neighbour uses it, default router password: 2 × 2 = **4 (low)**. Control: change the router password when convenient; accept for now.
Sorting by score gives a clear order of work: email first, payments second, backups third. When the coordinator asks "what should we spend on?", Amaka can show the numbers instead of guessing.

For each risk you have four choices. **Reduce** it with a control (most common). **Avoid** it by stopping the activity, for example no longer collecting ID numbers. **Transfer** part of it, for example by using a reputable cloud provider instead of a server under a desk. Or **accept** it, recording who accepted it and why. After a control is in place, score the risk again: the new, lower number is the **residual risk**, and it shows leaders what their spending achieved.
Your legal duties: the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023

Nigeria's main data protection law is the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA)**, which set up the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)** as the regulator. If an organisation collects personal data (names, phone numbers, ID numbers, health or financial details) it acts as a **data controller** and must follow the Act's principles. Security is not optional under the law; it is one of those principles.
**Lawful, fair and transparent:** have a lawful basis (such as consent or a contract) and tell people what you collect and why.
**Purpose limitation and data minimisation:** collect only what you need for a stated purpose. If you do not need someone's NIN, do not collect it.
**Accuracy and storage limitation:** keep data correct and delete it when it is no longer needed.
**Integrity and confidentiality:** protect data with appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as access control, encryption and training.
**Accountability:** be able to show what you did, which is why written policies and logs matter.

**Breach notification:** where a personal data breach is likely to put people's rights and freedoms at risk, the controller must notify the NDPC within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, and must inform affected people promptly where the risk is high.
Minimisation is the cheapest control
Data you never collected cannot leak. Reviewing your forms and deleting columns you do not use (for example, home addresses on an event sign-up sheet) reduces risk at zero cost.
Get proper advice for legal decisions

This lesson gives you a working understanding, not legal advice. For questions about a specific breach, contract or penalty, read the Act on the NDPC website and consult a qualified data protection officer or lawyer.

Three tools do most of the protective work for individuals and small teams: a **password manager**, **multi-factor authentication (MFA)** and **well-configured devices**. None of them is expensive. The skill at this level is choosing the right strength for each account and setting them up so that people actually keep using them.
Why length beats cleverness: the arithmetic

Password strength is about how many guesses an attacker would need. If a password is chosen at random, the number of possibilities is (number of choices per position) raised to the power of the length. A passphrase made of random words from the **EFF large wordlist** works the same way: the list has 7,776 words, one for every result of rolling five dice.
Worked example: comparing three passwords

For example, Chiamaka is choosing a master password for her new password manager. She compares three options, imagining an attacker who has stolen a leaked password file and can try 10 billion guesses per second. (This speed is illustrative; real speeds depend on how the website stored the password.)
8 random lowercase letters: 26^8 = 208,827,064,576 possibilities, about 209 billion. At 10 billion per second that is about 21 seconds to try them all.
4 random words from the EFF list: 7,776^4 = about 3.66 quadrillion (3.66 × 10^15). At the same speed that is about 366,000 seconds, roughly 4 days.
5 random words: 7,776^5 = about 2.84 × 10^19. That is about 2.84 billion seconds, or roughly 90 years.
In bits, each EFF word adds about 12.9 bits (because 2^12.9 is about 7,776), so 4 words are about 52 bits and 5 words about 65 bits.

Chiamaka chooses six random words, generated by dice or by the password manager itself, for her master passphrase. Each extra word multiplies the attacker's work by 7,776, which is far more than adding a symbol.

Notice what the example does not say: that you must memorise dozens of long passphrases. You memorise one strong master passphrase. The password manager generates and stores a unique random password for every other account, so a leak at one website cannot unlock another. Reused passwords, not short ones, are the biggest real-world cause of account takeover.
Choosing a password manager
**Bitwarden:** open source, works on Android, iPhone, Windows and in browsers, and has a free plan for individuals; also offers paid organisation plans with shared collections.

**Built-in managers** such as Google Password Manager (on Android and Chrome) and iCloud Keychain (on Apple devices): easy and free, good for people who will not install anything else, less suited to sharing across a team on mixed devices.
Whichever you choose: protect it with a long master passphrase, turn on MFA for the manager itself, and store the recovery code on paper in a safe place.

Read from the top: passkeys and security keys resist phishing, app codes are strong, SMS is better than nothing, and a password alone is the weakest.

**SMS codes** can be stolen through SIM swap fraud or tricked out of people on the phone. **Authenticator apps** such as Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator generate a six-digit code that changes every 30 seconds on the phone itself, which removes the SIM swap risk. **Passkeys** and **hardware security keys** (built on the FIDO standards) go further: the login only works on the real website, so a fake login page cannot capture anything useful. Use the strongest method each service offers, at least for email, banking, domain and social media admin accounts.

Tools on their own decay. Staff join and leave, phones are replaced, software goes out of date, and backups silently stop. Security leads therefore work in a **cycle**: they inventory, set a baseline, apply it, verify it, and repeat on a schedule. This lesson gives you that workflow for a team of roughly 3 to 20 people.
The hardening cycle
Inventory accounts and devices
Set the baseline
Apply and patch
Back up and test
Review and repeat
Run the full cycle once at the start, then review monthly for accounts and patches and quarterly for the whole baseline.
1. Inventory

Extend the asset list from Module 1 into a working register: every user account on each shared service (email, cloud storage, accounting, social media admin, website hosting, domain registrar), who has admin rights, and every device that touches organisational data, including personal phones used for work email.
2. Access control: least privilege

**Least privilege** means each person gets only the access their job needs. Most staff do not need to be admins of the Facebook page, the domain registrar or the Google Workspace account. Fewer admins means fewer high-value accounts for attackers to target. Use named accounts for every person; a shared login like office@ cannot tell you who did what and is rarely changed when someone leaves.
On the person's last day, disable or suspend their accounts rather than deleting them at once, so mail and files can be handed over.
Transfer ownership of their files and shared folders to a named colleague.
Remove them as admin from social media pages, the website and any bank or payment platform.
Change any shared password they knew, such as the office Wi-Fi.
Collect or remotely wipe organisation devices and sign them out of work accounts on personal devices.
Record the date and who completed each step.
Enforce, don't just ask

If the team uses Google Workspace, an administrator can enforce 2-Step Verification for everyone from the Admin console under Security settings, with a grace period for people to enrol. Microsoft 365 has similar controls. Enforcement turns a policy into a fact.
3. Patching

Updates fix security holes that attackers already know about. Turn on automatic updates for phones, laptops, browsers and apps. For a website built on WordPress or a similar platform, update the core, themes and plugins, and remove plugins you do not use. Old devices that no longer receive security updates should be retired from handling sensitive data.
4. Backups: the 3-2-1 rule

Backups are your answer to ransomware, theft and mistakes. The widely used **3-2-1 rule** says: keep **3** copies of important data, on **2** different types of storage, with **1** copy off-site. Ransomware can also encrypt any drive that is permanently connected, so at least one copy should be offline (a drive you unplug) or in a cloud service with version history that lets you roll back.
secure-server
A server rack with a shield symbol
A protected, separate copy of your data is what lets you recover without paying a ransom.
Worked example: sizing a 3-2-1 plan
For example, Hauwa runs IT for a 6-person consultancy in Kano. The shared project folder is 40 GB today and grows by about 2 GB a month.
Copy 1 is the working files on the office laptop and staff devices, synced to the team's cloud storage.
Copy 2 is cloud storage with version history. In 12 months the data will be 40 + (2 × 12) = 64 GB, so she chooses a plan with at least 100 GB, leaving 36 GB of headroom.
Copy 3 is a 1 TB external hard drive (a second storage type). On the last Friday of every month she copies the folder to it, unplugs it and takes it to the director's home (off-site and offline).
She writes the schedule into the shared calendar with a reminder.
Each quarter she tests: she picks three random files from the drive and one folder from the cloud's version history and restores them to a test folder, then opens each to confirm it works.

The team has three copies, two media types, one off-site and offline copy, and a recorded test every quarter. If ransomware hits the laptop, they lose at most about a month of work in the worst case, and usually far less thanks to cloud versions.
An untested backup is a hope, not a backup
Many organisations discover during an incident that their backup stopped months ago or cannot be opened. Record the date and result of each restore test in your audit log.
5. Review and repeat

Set a monthly 30-minute check: new or departed staff, admin list, devices missing updates, and backup status. Every quarter, rerun the full cycle and update the risk register scores. Over time you should see high scores fall as controls take effect.

Incident response plans, playbooks and the security log
Describe the four phases of the NIST incident response lifecycle
Follow a playbook for a compromised email account
Calculate reporting deadlines and record an incident timeline
Write a one-page incident response plan with contacts and roles

An **incident** is any event that threatens the confidentiality, integrity or availability of your information: a hacked account, a lost laptop, ransomware, a misdirected email with personal data. Incidents are stressful, and stressed people make poor decisions. An **incident response plan** written in advance tells everyone what to do, in what order, and who decides.
The NIST lifecycle

The most widely used framework comes from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology in its incident handling guide, SP 800-61. Its classic lifecycle has four phases that work for an organisation of any size.
Phase
What it means for a small team
Preparation
Plan, contacts, playbooks, backups and logs ready before anything happens
Detection and analysis
Notice the signs, confirm what happened, decide how serious it is, start the log
Containment, eradication and recovery
Stop the spread, remove the attacker's access, restore clean systems and data
Post-incident activity
Lessons-learned meeting within about two weeks; update controls, plan and risk register
First 72 hours of a data breach
Hour 0: detected, log started
Hours 0 to 2: contain
Hours 2 to 24: analyse scope
By hour 72: notify NDPC if required
Week 2: lessons learned
Containment comes first; the 72-hour NDPC clock starts when the organisation becomes aware of a reportable breach.
server-down
A person looking at a server that has failed
When systems fail or are attacked, a written plan replaces panic with clear next steps.
Playbook: a compromised email account

A **playbook** is a short, specific checklist for one type of incident. Email takeover is the most common incident small teams face, so write this one first. Work from a clean device, not the one you suspect.
Sign in from a clean device and change the password to a new unique one from the password manager.
Sign out all other sessions (in a Google account, use the security page to review devices and sign them out).
Check and remove unknown forwarding addresses, filters and auto-reply rules.
Check recovery email and phone number; correct any that were changed.
Turn on or re-register MFA, preferably an authenticator app or passkey, and revoke unknown connected apps.
Review the Sent folder and deleted items to see what the attacker sent, and warn contacts who may have received fraudulent messages.
Decide whether personal data was exposed; if so, assess whether it must be reported to the NDPC.
Record every action with time and name in the incident log.
Preserve evidence before you clean up
Before deleting malicious rules or emails, take screenshots showing the date, time and details. Banks, the police and regulators may need them, and they help you understand how the attacker got in.
Worked example: an incident timeline with deadlines

For example, Ifeoma is the volunteer IT lead for a Lagos parents' association that keeps a spreadsheet of 420 families with names, phone numbers and children's classes. On Tuesday at 14:00 a committee member reports she clicked a link and "signed in to Google" on a strange page.
14:00 Tuesday: Ifeoma opens the incident log and records the report. This is the moment of awareness.

14:20: from her own laptop she helps the member change the password, sign out all sessions and check for rules. She finds a forwarding rule sending all mail to an unknown address, screenshots it, then removes it.
15:30: checking the account activity, she sees the attacker opened the shared drive, and the family spreadsheet was shared with the member's account.
She judges this a personal data breach that may put families at risk (phone numbers plus children's details could enable targeted scams).
Deadline calculation: awareness Tuesday 14:00 + 72 hours = Friday 14:00. She drafts the NDPC notification with the chair on Wednesday and submits it Thursday morning, well within time.
Wednesday: the association messages parents through its usual channel, explaining what happened, what data was involved, and warning them to ignore calls asking for money or codes.

The breach was contained within 20 minutes, the regulator was notified in time, and families were warned. At the lessons-learned meeting the committee agreed to require 2-Step Verification for everyone and to limit the spreadsheet to two named people.
Who to call: your contact sheet
Internal: incident lead, backup lead, the person who can approve spending and speak publicly.
Banks and payment providers: the fraud or 24-hour lines, saved in advance.
Platform support: Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 admin, website host, domain registrar.
Nigeria's national CERT (ngCERT), which handles cyber incident reports, and the NDPC for personal data breaches.
The police, for fraud or extortion such as ransomware demands.
The security log

Keep one simple log in a sheet: date and time, what happened, who reported it, actions taken, by whom, and status. Log near misses too, such as a phishing email someone reported. Over months the log shows patterns, proves accountability under the NDPA, and gives you real evidence for your next risk review.

Security discovery: authorisation, interviews and finding the real gaps
Explain why written authorisation must come before any security review
Run a discovery interview using a structured question set
Measure control coverage with simple percentages
Turn discovery notes into prioritised findings

When you review someone else's security, the first and most important document is not a technical report. It is a **written authorisation**: a signed note or email from someone with authority, stating what you may look at, which systems, during which dates, and what you must not do. Without it, even well-meant checking can cross a legal line.
Never test without permission

Nigeria's Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act 2015 makes unauthorised access to computer systems an offence. Do not try to log in to accounts, scan networks or send test phishing emails for any organisation unless you have clear written permission that covers exactly that activity.
The discovery flow
From first call to findings
Signed authorisation and scope
Interview the leader
Interview staff and admins
Check settings together
Score and prioritise findings
Each stage builds on the last; checking settings only happens with the account owner present and with permission.

At this level discovery is mostly conversation and observation, not hacking. You learn how the organisation really works, where the money and personal data flow, and which controls exist on paper but not in practice. A good consultant asks open questions, listens, and confirms by looking at settings together with the owner.
interview
Two people sitting across a table having a structured conversation
Most security gaps are discovered by asking good questions and then checking the answers together.

Area
Questions to ask
What you look for
People and roles

Too many admins, shared logins, one person with all the keys

MFA gaps on email and finance; SMS-only MFA

Unneeded data, spreadsheets shared with "anyone with the link"

Which devices hold work data? Are personal phones used? Are updates on?
Unlocked phones, old unsupported laptops, pirated software

Worked example: discovery at a private school

For example, Zainab is invited to review security at a private primary school in Ibadan with 14 staff email accounts. The proprietor signs a one-page authorisation covering interviews and a joint review of Google Workspace and Facebook settings for two weeks, and excluding any testing of the school's bank portal.
She interviews the proprietor (30 minutes), the bursar and the admin officer (20 minutes each).
With the admin officer beside her, she opens the Workspace admin console and counts accounts with 2-Step Verification on: 11 of 14. Coverage = 11 ÷ 14 = 0.786, about 79%.
She counts super admins: 4 people, including a teacher who left last term. Target: 2.
She finds the pupils' records spreadsheet shared as "anyone with the link can view".
The bursar confirms bank-detail changes are accepted by email with no call-back.
She scores each finding with the likelihood and impact matrix from Module 1.

Her top findings: (1) open link to pupil records, score 4 × 5 = 20; (2) no payment call-back rule, 3 × 5 = 15; (3) a departed teacher still a super admin, 3 × 5 = 15; (4) three accounts without 2-Step Verification, 4 × 4 = 16. Each comes with a specific fix and owner.
Writing findings people act on

Each finding should have five parts: a short title, what you observed (fact, not opinion), why it matters in plain words, the risk score, and a recommended fix with an owner and a date. Avoid fear language and blame. "The pupil spreadsheet is visible to anyone with the link" is a fact; "your staff are careless" is not a finding.
Lead with the two or three highest risks; leaders rarely read past the first page.
Separate quick wins (under an hour, no cost) from projects that need budget or time.
Never put passwords, recovery codes or full personal data in your report. Describe them instead.
Store your notes securely and delete client data you no longer need when the engagement ends.

Discovery can be done on site or over a video call, but checking settings works best in person with the account owner driving the screen. You watch and take notes; they click. This keeps passwords with their owner, avoids you holding admin access you do not need, and teaches them where the settings live so they can maintain them after you leave.

Close discovery with a short meeting to read back what you heard. Leaders often correct small misunderstandings at this stage ("actually the bursar has a second bank login"), which saves you from writing wrong findings. Agree the date for your written report before you leave.
Measure so you can show progress
Simple percentages like MFA coverage, number of admins, and days since last restore test let you show improvement at the follow-up visit: for example, from 79% to 100% coverage.

Whether you work as an employee, a volunteer lead or an independent consultant, you need to describe security work in terms a manager can approve: what will be done, how long it takes, what it costs and what it will not cover. Clear scope protects both sides, and in security it also protects you legally.

The hours above are an example for a team of about 10 to 15 people with one email platform and simple systems. Larger teams, more platforms or messy records take longer. Track your actual hours on each job so your future estimates come from your own data.
Worked example: calculating a fee

For example, Zainab prepares a proposal for the Ibadan school from Lesson 1. She uses an hourly rate of 8,000 naira, which is purely illustrative here; your rate depends on your experience, location and the client.
Total hours: 6 + 10 + 4 + 3 = 23 hours.
Base fee: 23 × 8,000 = 184,000 naira.
Contingency of 15% for unknowns: 184,000 × 0.15 = 27,600 naira.
Subtotal: 184,000 + 27,600 = 211,600 naira, which she rounds to 212,000 naira.
Costs the client pays directly are listed separately, not hidden in her fee: for example, a cloud storage plan and an external backup drive at approximate market prices.
Payment terms: 50% (106,000 naira) on signing, 50% on delivery of the report.
The school sees a clear total of 212,000 naira for her work, a separate list of tools to buy, and exactly what each phase delivers. Rounding and contingency are explained, so there are no surprises.

Handling change requests

Midway through, the proprietor may ask, "While you are here, can you also look at the bursar's laptop and set up the new website?" That is normal. Reply warmly, write the request down, estimate the extra hours and cost, and get approval in writing before starting. A one-paragraph change note is enough. This keeps the relationship friendly and stops unpaid work growing silently.
Never promise total security

No honest professional can guarantee that an organisation will never be breached. Promise specific, checkable actions ("all accounts will have 2-Step Verification") and explain that these reduce risk significantly. Overpromising damages trust and may create liability.

Leading awareness training, building a portfolio and choosing certifications
Plan and deliver a 60 to 90 minute security awareness session
Measure behaviour change with before and after numbers
Assemble an anonymised security portfolio
Choose a realistic next certification and 90-day plan

Technology fixes stop many attacks, but people still receive the phishing emails, approve the payments and lose the phones. A security lead who can teach colleagues clearly is valuable in any organisation. This lesson shows you how to lead that learning, prove it worked, and present your growing experience professionally.
Designing an awareness session that changes behaviour
Start with a real, anonymised story from the organisation's own risk register or log, not frightening statistics.
Teach three behaviours only, for example: check the real sender, call back on numbers on file, report anything odd at once.
Show, then do: everyone checks their own account's 2-Step Verification and recovery details during the session.
Practise with examples: show three real-looking emails and let the group decide which is fraudulent and why.
Make reporting easy and blame-free: one WhatsApp number or email address for reporting, and thanks for every report.
End with a one-page reminder sheet and a date for a short follow-up.
teaching
A person presenting to a small group in front of a board
Short, hands-on sessions where people secure their own accounts change behaviour more than long lectures.
Simulated phishing needs permission

Some organisations send practice phishing emails to staff. Only do this with written approval from leadership, tell staff in general terms that exercises may happen, and use results to teach, never to shame or punish individuals.
Worked example: measuring the effect of training
For example, Ngozi leads security for a 20-person NGO in Port Harcourt. Before her session she records three baseline numbers from the admin console and the security log.
Before: 9 of 20 staff had 2-Step Verification, which is 9 ÷ 20 = 45%. In the previous month staff reported 1 suspicious email.
During the 75-minute session, staff enable 2-Step Verification together; 8 more turn it on in the room.
One week later, 3 more have enrolled with help: 9 + 8 + 3 = 20 of 20, which is 100%.
In the month after training, staff report 7 suspicious emails. Reports went from 1 to 7, which she treats as a good sign: people are noticing and speaking up, not that attacks increased sevenfold.
She records all numbers in the log and in a short note to the director.
Ngozi can show leadership a clear result: MFA coverage rose from 45% to 100% and reporting became normal. This becomes a strong portfolio case study.

Adapt the session to your audience. Many staff in small organisations are most comfortable in Pidgin, Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa or another local language, and some read slowly. Use spoken explanations, large screenshots of the exact screens they will see, and a short voice note summary they can replay on WhatsApp. Pair confident staff with those who need help during the hands-on part, so nobody is left behind or embarrassed.

Leadership is continuous, not a single event. Send one short reminder a month linked to something real, such as a new scam pattern reported by a colleague, and thank the people who reported it. Ask leaders to go first when a new control arrives, for example enrolling in 2-Step Verification in front of the team. When the director follows the rule, everyone else does too.
Building your portfolio

Employers and clients want evidence. Your course audit already contains most of what you need. Turn it into two or three case studies, each one or two pages, with every identifying detail removed or changed with permission: no organisation name unless they agree, no names of staff, no screenshots showing emails, IDs or personal data.
**The situation:** type and size of organisation, the main concern.
**What you did:** discovery, risk register, controls applied, training.
**Results in numbers:** MFA coverage, admins reduced, backups tested, reporting rate.
**Documents:** an anonymised risk register, an incident plan template, your awareness reminder sheet.
**A short reference:** with permission, a line from the client or manager.
